title: Knock and greet
hook: don't enter houses until you've asked permission and greeted the people (24:27)
tomorrow: Don't you want to be forgiven?

segments.voice: Yesterday, lower the gaze, and your line was guard the eyes. Which second look did you let go? Day four hundred ninety-five.

Commentators on this verse describe an older habit. A visitor would walk straight into a house and call out a greeting once already inside, good morning, to someone who might not be ready to be seen. Sometimes a curtain was all that stood in the way. Surah An-Nur, a surah full of rules about privacy and dignity, sets down a small one about thresholds. It's so ordinary you could miss how much it says. Today, the knock.

Verse twenty-seven. Pickthall begins: "O ye who believe! Enter not houses other than your own". And then: not until you've made yourselves known, and greeted the people inside with peace. The verb for making yourself known is tasta'nisu. Commentators link it to uns, the word for ease, friendliness, feeling at home with someone. So it isn't only asking permission. It's waiting until the people inside are comfortable with you being there. Then the next verse adds: if you find no one at home, don't go in. And if you're told to go back, go back. That is purer for you. No argument, no peering through the window. The hadith fill in the picture. Bukhari records Abu Musa going to 'Umar's house, asking permission three times, getting no answer, and leaving. When 'Umar later asked why he'd left, Abu Musa said the Prophet ﷺ taught: ask permission three times, and if you're not given it, go back. Another report, in Abu Dawud, says that when the Prophet came to someone's door, he would stand to one side of it, not facing straight in, and give the greeting. That's the whole lesson in a posture. Stand where you can't see in. Say peace. Wait. So knock and greet isn't fussy etiquette. It's a picture of respect for another person's space, the part of their life they get to decide about. Today the doors have locks and the houses have bells, but the same idea reaches a bedroom door, a phone left on a table, a message thread that isn't yours.
screen: `ENTER NOT HOUSES NOT YOUR OWN.` · `TASTA'NISU: UNTIL THEY'RE AT EASE.` · `ASK THREE TIMES, THEN GO BACK.` · `STAND TO ONE SIDE OF THE DOOR.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: knock and wait. Sit, and let the breath settle. Think of the doors you go through without knocking. A family member's room. A colleague's desk. A friend's phone, a shared screen. Picture yourself standing beside one of them, knocking, and waiting, a few breaths longer than feels natural, until you're welcome. If you pray, you can say the greeting of peace to yourself as you picture it. The bell holds the time.
Knock and greet. Make yourself known, say peace, and wait until you're welcome. If you're told to go back, go back. Today's word.
Your line: ask before entering. Today, knock on one door you'd usually walk straight through, and wait for the answer. Day four hundred ninety-five.

howItsDone: Muslim families often teach children to knock, say as-salamu 'alaykum and wait before entering a room, following 24:27–28 and the hadith on asking permission three times.

fork.setup: you've come to a friend's house. you've called out a greeting three times. no answer. what do you do?
options: look through the window to check.
fork.reveal: go back. Abu Musa did exactly this at 'Umar's house, citing the Prophet: ask three times, then return.

original.note: Arabic: make yourselves known, until there is ease; from uns, familiarity. 24:27.

trapdoor: what you thought: knock before you go in.
what it means: make yourself known, greet with peace, and wait until the people inside are at ease; if turned away, go back.
what a scholar hears: tasta'nisu (from uns) rather than the expected tasta'dhinu (ask permission); Abu Musa and 'Umar in Bukhari 6245; standing beside the door in Abu Dawud 5186.

notes: Pickthall wording of the opening of 24:27 quoted from memory; please confirm.
The hook's claim that many houses had curtains rather than doors is a common explanation in commentaries on 24:27; confirm or soften.
Tasta'nisu as from uns (ease, familiarity): confirm with a lexicon; some commentators equate it with tasta'dhinu.
Hadith numbers (Bukhari 6245, Abu Dawud 5186) cited from memory; confirm.

Editor review 2026-10-01: hook no longer asserts a date and 'many houses had no doors'; it now attributes the pre-Islamic habit of walking in and greeting from inside to commentators on 24:27; the uns derivation is attributed to commentators.
